implementation_notes: On the JVM the pattern is an element collection: the child type is @Embeddable, the parent holds it in an @ElementCollection mapped to a @CollectionTable, and the persistence provider loads, inserts and deletes those rows as part of persisting the entity - there is no finder, no repository and no identity for the element. Providers commonly rewrite the collection by deleting and re-inserting its rows on update, which is exactly the pattern's replacement semantics; Spring Data JDBC formalizes the same idea, persisting the children of an aggregate with the root and deleting and recreating them on save, with only the root having a repository. The classic structure is right whenever the element type must not be queried on its own.
pitfalls: On update the provider deletes all collection rows and re-inserts them: element row identity churns, and any other table referencing those rows breaks.
FetchType.LAZY is only a hint and the collection is always reached through the parent; detached entities throw LazyInitializationException unless the use case fetches the collection explicitly.
Dropping the element type's own repository is the discipline: an em.createQuery over OrderLine reintroduces the independent lifecycle the pattern removes.
